news_revere.title: Revere Housing Trust Launches Buy Down Program for Homebuyers
news_revere.author: Jim Mitchell
news_revere.summary:
By Barbara Taormina

 

The Affordable Housing Trust Fund Board is gearing up for their next big program to make homeownership possible for low-to-moderate-income buyers. The board’s Buy Down program is a pilot homeownership assistance initiative that will help eligible households close the gap between market prices and what is considered affordable in exchange for deed restrictions and profit sharing with the trust. The Buy Down program reduces the difference between the sales price of a home and an affordable price for low-to-moderate-income buyers. It differs from the down payment assistance program, which is a flat $10,000 grant. The board has acknowledged that the $10,000 down payment has not kept pace with local home sales prices. The Buy Down program is unique because it will lower the purchase price and create genuine affordability.

The board is aiming to create deed-restricted, owner-occupied homes while supporting Revere families who are priced out of the current market. Homes purchased through the Buy Down program will carry a deed restriction for the first 10 years. If the home is resold, it must be resold at an affordable price. From 10 to 20 years, if there is a profit from the sale of the home, the homeowner and Trust split the profit. After 20 years, the homeowner owns the property outright with no affordability restrictions.

The Buy Down program is funded by the Affordable Housing Trust, the Community Development Block Grant and state assistance with a capped amount of help per household.

At their meeting earlier this month, the board discussed advertising the program and designing the applications to be eligible for the program applicants — must have a local connection, such as two years of residency in Revere or have a child in the Revere school system. Applicants must also fall into the low-to-moderate-income range. Applications will be accepted on a rolling basis and will be available in English, Spanish, Portuguese and Arabic.

Board members plan to engage local banks and lenders in Revere, so they understand the program and can work with its requirements. They also intend to blanket the city with flyers, light up social media with information and do whatever it takes to get the word out to residents who might benefit from this opportunity.

Applications for the Buy Down program are expected to be available this fall.

news_revere.title: Kelly Announces Retirement as Superintendent
news_revere.author: Journal Staff
news_revere.summary:
By Adam Swift

After nearly a dozen years leading the district and three decades in the Revere school system, Superintendent of Schools Dr. Dianne Kelly has announced her intention to retire next July.

In a letter to the school committee, Kelly said she intends to retire on July 6 of next year. She stated that giving nearly a year’s notice will give the committee ample time to thoughtfully plan for the transition and identify the best person to next lead the Revere Public Schools.

“Serving the Revere community has been one of the greatest honors and privileges of my professional life,” Kelly stated. “By the time of my retirement, I will have dedicated 32 years to the Revere Public Schools; 12 years as superintendent. Throughout my career, I have had the opportunity to work alongside exceptional educators, staff, students, families, city leaders, and School Committee members who share an unwavering commitment to providing the highest quality education for every child.”

Kelly began her career in the Revere Public Schools in 1995 as a mathematics teacher at the high school.  While in the classroom, she also served as President of the Revere Teachers Association and Lead Teacher of the Mathematics Department. Prior to being named Superintendent, Kelly served in several other administrative positions including Dean of Students at Revere High School; District Director of Mathematics; District Director of Math, Science, and Technology; and Assistant Superintendent.

“Dr. Kelly has been the cornerstone of Revere’s educational success over the last decade, and will leave very big shoes to fill,” said Mayor Patrick Keefe, who also serves as the chair of the school committee. “I am confident that over the next year we will determine her successor, and expect Dr. Kelly to help support the eventual transition, as I know she wants to leave Revere in capable and competent hands. We have a lot of work ahead and look forward to supporting Dr. Kelly finishing out her legacy in Revere. 

“It’s too early to touch base on the personal accolades but, in short, she is irreplaceable in many ways, however as we know, change is constant.”

Kelly said she is proud of the district and school committee’s many accomplishments, especially getting the construction of the new Revere High School underway.

“However, I am even more proud of the relationships we have built and the positive impact our collective efforts have had on generations of Revere students,” Kelly stated. “The progress our district has made over the past three decades is the result of dedicated teamwork, thoughtful leadership, and a shared vision for excellence. I am confident that Revere Public Schools is well positioned for continued success, and I know the next Superintendent will inherit a district filled with talented professionals and a community that deeply values public education.”

In her letter to the school committee, Kelly thanked every member she has worked with for the trust, support, and partnership that they have extended to her throughout her tenure.

“I remain fully committed to leading the district over the coming year, ensuring a smooth and successful leadership transition,” Kelly stated. “I look forward to working closely with the School Committee throughout this process and to finishing my career with the same dedication and enthusiasm that has guided me for the past three decades.”

news_revere.title: Council to Hold Public Hearing on Public Naming Ordinance
news_revere.author: Journal Staff
news_revere.summary:
By Adam Swift

The city council will hold a public hearing on a new ordinance for naming public municipal buildings at its meeting on Monday, July 27.

The ordinance was proposed to provide more concrete guidelines for the city, and closely mirrors the one recently enacted by the school committee, according to Rose Burns, aide to Mayor Patrick Keefe.

Burns presented the ordinance to the council at its regular meeting last week.

“It is some housekeeping that aims to establish a consistent, historically accurate, and meaningful process in naming and renaming city property,” said Burns. “This ordinance aims to mirror the school department’s pre-existing charter, with consistent and collaborative guidelines moving forward that maintain accordance (with state law).”

Several councilors stated that they would like to see the ordinance apply to school buildings as well as municipal buildings. However, Ward 3 Councillor Anthony Cogliandro noted that the ordinance proposed by the city mirrors the ordinance that was already approved by the school committee, and that they are effectively similar.

Several councillors also said they would like to see the ordinance revised to allow buildings to be named for people who have been dead for a shorter time than proposed. The ordinance calls for a 10-year window after someone dies before naming a building or property after them.

“I was just curious how the mayor’s office came to the conclusion of 10 years and not an age,” said Councillor-at-Large Robert Haas, III.

Burns noted that it was only a suggestion for the language from the mayor’s office, and that it could be discussed further at the public hearing and by the council.

“We just want to make sure that any property … a significant building with someone’s name on it is named after someone who had a significant impact on the city and stood the test of time,” said Burns. “I think 10 years is a decent sense of time, but obviously, that is something that if we want to, we can have a further discussion about it.”

Cogliandro said he personally believed the 10-year mark was too long, but said he understood there would be further discussion on the issue. Ward 1 Councillor Jim Mercurio said he believed that five years would be a more appropriate marker.

news_revere.title: News Brief
news_revere.author: Journal Staff
news_revere.summary:
Final Night of Revere Street Paving Operations in Winthrop

Commuters traveling between Revere and Winthrop should prepare for traffic delays as Winthrop concludes its overnight paving on Revere Street. Work begins at 7 p.m. on Wednesday, July 22, and wraps up by 7 a.m. on Thursday.

To minimize daytime disruption for local commerce, heavy construction on this major thoroughfare is strictly limited to overnight hours. However, drivers should expect significant delays and localized detours during the active paving windows.

Police details and signage will actively direct traffic throughout the work zone. Authorities strongly advise that all motorists seek alternate routes until the project is successfully completed tomorrow morning.

Chelsea Square Activates with Film Screening and Weekend Car Show

Chelsea is continuing its “Summer in the Square” program, transforming Chelsea Square into a dynamic hub of civic engagement. On Thursday, July 23, at 6:00 PM, residents can enjoy a free outdoor screening of Jaws on a massive LED screen provided by Eastern Salt Company.

The weekend brings the Discover Chelsea Car Show & Market on Saturday, July 25, from 2:00 PM to 6:00 PM. Presented in partnership with the Chelsea Chamber of Commerce, the event will feature classic cars, live entertainment, and local food vendors.

To prioritize pedestrian safety, 2nd Street will be closed between Park Street and Broadway. All events are free, and attendees are encouraged to bring their own chairs and patronize the surrounding local businesses.

Revere Beach Summer Farmers Market Resumes Operations

The Revere Beach Farmers Market officially returns for its summer season this Saturday, July 25. Operating weekly from 11:00 AM to 3:00 PM, the market brings local agriculture and artisanal goods directly to the waterfront.

This market directly addresses urban food insecurity by participating in programs like SNAP/EBT and the Healthy Incentives Program (HIP). It allows residents to easily access fresh, local produce while retaining economic capital within the immediate community.

The market also serves as a vibrant community destination. With live entertainment scheduled each week—including the band “The Twos” performing this Saturday—the event seamlessly blends local commerce with cultural recreation.

City Council to Evaluate Zoning Expansion for Body Art and Food Trucks

The Revere City Council will hold a public hearing on Monday, July 27, at 6:00 PM in the City Council Chambers to discuss proposed zoning revisions. The primary focus is on expanding the operational boundaries for body art establishments and mobile food vendors.

Historically limited to specific districts, these niche businesses could soon see increased zoning flexibility across the city. The proposed ordinance changes aim to lower bureaucratic barriers, activate underutilized spaces, and stimulate independent economic activity.

Residents and stakeholders will have the opportunity to weigh in on Monday evening. The hearing will explore how Revere can best balance traditional neighborhood characteristics with the integration of modern, agile enterprises.

Constitution Beach to Host Annual Eastie Beach Bash

Save the Harbor/Save the Bay will host its highly anticipated Eastie Beach Bash on Wednesday, July 29, from 10:00 AM to 1:00 PM at Constitution Beach in East Boston. The free event typically draws hundreds of youth and families from across Greater Boston, including Revere, Chelsea, and Winthrop.

Designed to foster environmental literacy, the Bash offers interactive experiences like instructional fishing, kayaking, and a live crab touch tank. These hands-on activities are paired with traditional beach fun, such as sandcastle building and face painting.

By removing financial and logistical barriers, the event helps urban youth build a lasting connection with the region’s marine environment. It continues to serve as a strong model for inclusive coastal recreation and ecological education.

news_revere.title: Video and Drone Cameras Assist with Water Rescue
news_revere.author: Journal Staff
news_revere.summary:
Staff Report

Emergency personnel used drone video and live camera feeds to help rescue two people struggling in the water near the breakers at Eliot Circle on Sunday afternoon.

Shortly before 1 p.m. on Sunday, the regional dispatch center got a call reporting two people struggling in the water near the breakers.

Because the incident happened during the Revere Beach International Sand Sculpting Festival, police and fire personnel working the event detail also responded.

Public Safety personnel at the festival Unified Command Center used drone video from Revere Police, live cameras along the festival site from State Police, and information from the regional dispatch center to ascertain the location of the people.

With the assistance from the Massachusetts State Police Marine Unit, the fire department used its Zodiac watercraft to get out to the stranded people and safely get them to shore.  The two people were assessed by Cataldo Ambulance Service and released, according to fire officials.

news_revere.title: Council Approves Outdoor Lighting Ordinance
news_revere.author: Journal Staff
news_revere.summary:
By Adam Swift

Last week, the city council approved an ordinance that sets fines for nuisance outdoor lighting.

The council approved a version that was successfully amended by Ward 3 Councillor Anthony Cogliandro that lowered the fines for the nuisance lighting from $300 to $50 if the issue was not addressed by property owners.

“Myself and Councillor (Joanne) McKenna, we heard the council’s recommendations loud and clear,” said Cogliandro. “We know that there are still some issues with it, but we did change – if there is an issue with lighting and someone has to pull a permit to update it, that will not trigger other issues in the home that are grandfathered in and have to be renovated. The holiday lighting portion of the ordinance was removed, as well as if there is a complaint made on someone’s home, they now have 21 days to hire an electrician or have one come into their home to fix the issue before there are any sorts of fines.”

Ward 4 Councillor Paul Argenzio asked what the process would be to determine a violation through the inspectional services department, since that department does not have staff that works at night.

“I would assume that like many other things in the city, that if there is a complaint made, they would have to provide proof,” said Cogliandro. “For instance, if someone’s light is shining directly into your yard – which I really think is going to be the major issue that we potentially solve with this – someone takes a picture or a video and sends it in as evidence. We have to do the same thing with … noise complaints, illegal building, things like that.

“It’s a great point that they don’t work at night, but I am sure with evidence they could contact that person and say turn lights off, point them down, solve the issue quickly.”

Cogliandro also noted that the ordinance would not apply to the city’s outdoor athletic fields.

During last week’s zoning subcommittee meeting on the issue, Councillor-at-Large Michelle Kelley said she thought the amendments made to the proposed ordinance were great, but that she still could not support the ordinance because of its subjectivity and enforcement difficulty.

“The glare aspect is something that can probably only be seen at night,” said Kelley. “To me, it is too subjective – when does that raise an issue, how much glare is going to be a problem? I think it’s still too subjective, so that’s the concern that I have now.”

Kelley and Ward 2 Councilor Ira Novoselsky voted against the ordinance at the regular council meeting following the subcommittee meeting. Novoselsky also raised concerns about enforcement of the ordinance.

news_revere.title: BK’s Bar and Grill Voluntarily Rolls Back Hours After incidents
news_revere.author: Journal Staff
news_revere.summary:
By Journal Staff

The Revere License Commission held its regular monthly meeting last Wednesday, July 15, in the City Council Chamber. On hand for the session were Chair Robert Selevitch, Daniel Occena, and Liliana Monroy.

The first item on the agenda was an application from Royal Food Enterprises, Inc., d/b/a La Abuela Carmen Products, 91 Centennial Avenue, Mohammed Fdal, for a  change of DBA to La Abuela Carmen Products from Crown Fried Chicken & Pizza. All operations will remain the same.

Mr. Fdal appeared before the commission and explained that the business will revert to its original concept as a bakery rather than a chicken and pizza place.

The commission unanimously approved the application.

The commissioners then held a hearing pertaining to, “State Police complaints of numerous disruptions, service to intoxicated patrons, assaults, and fights” at BK’s Bar & Grill, 264 Ocean Avenue.

Robert Kelly, the owner and manager of the establishment, did not deny the allegations, but stated that he has taken steps proactively in an effort to address the problem by closing at 1:00 AM instead of 2:00 AM on Friday and Saturday nights.

Kelly noted that the problems stem from patrons who come from other communities which have a 1:00 AM closing time. He also said that he has let go security staff who had been allowing patrons to enter the bar after the doors should have been closed to new customers.

Sgt. Edward Troy from the State Police told the commissioners of a fight that had occurred recently, as well as other incidents involving fights outside the premises, including that of an alleged underage drinker who had been beaten.

Sgt. Troy informed the commissioners of measures that the bar has taken to ensure that IDs are being checked and that patrons are not being overserved.

“Are the State Police satisfied that the bar owner has taken appropriate steps to rectify the problems?” asked Selevitch.

“It’s been a short time, but it appears that it has been much better,” Sgt. Troy replied.

Revere Police Lieut. Glenn Malley suggested that having a police detail would help to alleviate the problem, a suggestion that Kelly said he was open to when the establishment eventually returns to its 2:00 AM closing hours, though Kelly said he has no intention of doing so for the immediate future.

The members voted to place the matter “on file” and will address it in the future if there are any future incidents.

The commission heard an application from Black Marble Motorcycles, LLC, d/b/a Boston Harley-Davidson, 649 Squire Road, for a 1-day Common Victualler and Entertainment License to be exercised from 10 a.m. – 12 p.m. on Saturday, August 15, for a Breakfast, Beats & Bikes event. The expected attendance is 100.

Gabrielle Einstein, the event manager, presented the application. Ms. Einstein said there will be a DJ and a breakfast food truck. The motorcycles will be stationary and will not be operated.

There were no opponents and the commission unanimously approved the license.

Los Compadres Oaxaquenos, LLC, d/b/a B & M Grill, 843 Broadway

Manuel J. Hernandez, manager, submitted an application for a change of hours and to amend its entertainment hours on Friday and Saturday to 10 a.m. – 1 a.m., and for a change of hours of karaoke entertainment to Friday – Saturday 7

p.m. – 11 p.m. The current closing hour is midnight and current karaoke hours are Saturday 6 p.m. – 10 p.m.

Danvers Atty. Richard Mestone presented the application. Mr. Hernandez also attended the hearing. Atty. Mestone said that the business has been open since 2020 and they are looking to expand the Friday and Saturday alcohol service to 1:00 AM and the karaoke until 11:00 p.m.

There were no opponents and the commissioners did not have any questions. The application was unanimously approved.

The Chill House, Inc., 435 Revere Street, Jason Calnan, manager, applied for a Common Victualler license to serve ice cream. The requested hours of operation are Sunday – Saturday from 12 p.m. – 10 p.m. with no requested seating.

Mr. Calnan presented the application. He said he will be serving gelato and soft-serve ice cream There were no opponents and the commissioners unanimously approved the application subject to the establishment obtaining the appropriate approvals from the city.

Rappi Doggie’s, LLC, 61 Squire Road, Evan Andrew Long, operator, filed an application for a Stationary Mobile Food Vendor License to be operated at 61 Squire Road (which presently is a vacant parking lot) from Sunday–Saturday from 4:30 p.m.–1 a.m. with outdoor seating for 16 patrons.

Mr. Long presented the application. He said his truck serves Venezuelan fast food, as well as hot dogs, french fries, and ice tea. There were no opponents and the commissioners unanimously approved the application.

The commission heard an application from Las Parceritas, Diana Cardona, event manager, for a 1-day entertainment license to be exercised at McMackin Veterans Memorial Park on Thursday, July 23, from 3 p.m.–7:30 p.m. for a celebration of Colombian Independence Day. The expected attendance is 60.

Ms. Cardona told the commissioners that the event will feature singers, a DJ, and cultural events, as well as vendors for food and arts & crafts. She said the event was held last year without any incidents.

The commission unanimously approved the application.

City Diner Corporation, 361 Broadway, Brayan Medina Barrera, manager, presented an application for the transfer of a Common Victualler and Entertainment license from The Good Diner, LLC.

The requested seating will remain at 19 inside and eight outside. The requested hours will remain on Monday – Thursday from 7 a.m. – 11 p.m. and Friday – Sunday 24 hours and the requested entertainment will remain Widescreen Cable TV, and Radio.

The commissioners unanimously approved the application.

The final item on the agenda was a hearing “into violations of Fire and Building safety codes, and failure to maintain sufficient facilities for the number of cars on the license” by Atlantic Autobody, Inc., 529 Broadway, Ana Rita F. Sarnaglia, manager. The hearing had been continued from the May meeting.

Cleison Sarnaglia spoke on behalf of the establishment. Mr. Sarnaglia updated the commission on the progress he is making to remedy the various issues he is facing. The commission also received an email from the Revere Fire Dept. stating that Mr. Sarnaglia is moving ahead with remedying the violations.

The commission voted to take no action at this time and will await word of further progress in the situation.

The next meeting of the commission is set for August 19.

news_revere.title: Healey Takes Action to Cut Concert, Sports Ticket Resale and Fees
news_revere.author: Journal Staff
news_revere.summary:
Special to the Journal

Gov. Maura Healey has announced that she will file An Act Relative to Closing the Great Divide between Ticket Prices and Affordability, or The Great Divide Act, to lower sports and concert ticket resale prices and ensure that fans have a fair opportunity to enjoy the events they love without paying exorbitant prices on the secondary market. The legislation would establish some of the nation’s strongest consumer protections for the secondary ticket marketplace, building on reforms recently adopted in states such as Vermont and Maine.

The Governor’s proposal, which will be included in her upcoming closeout supplemental budget, caps the resale price of concert tickets at 110 percent of the price of the face value of the original ticket. It also limits the service fees and charges that can be imposed by ticket resellers like StubHub and SeatGeek to no more than 10 percent of the total price of the ticket for resale. It prohibits the sale of speculative tickets, which are tickets that are not in the possession of the seller when they are listed for sale. Finally, it implements additional consumer protections measures, including prohibiting the use of deceptive websites by ticket resellers and misleading consumers about the availability of tickets.  

The name of the proposal is a nod to singer and songwriter Noah Kahan, who recently made history as the first artist ever to headline four consecutive sold-out shows at Fenway Park. Kahan has been a vocal opponent against predatory resale practices and successfully advocated for a similar bill in Vermont.

“Far too many Massachusetts residents have experienced the pain of being excited to buy tickets to see their favorite singer or sports team, only to realize that resale prices and fees have driven up the cost to outrageous levels,” said Governor Healey. “Or how about when you do purchase tickets from a reseller, only to get to the venue to realize the seller never actually transfers them to you? Enough is enough. We are taking action to lower ticket resale prices so Massachusetts fans can better afford to see their favorite performer or team.”

During the press conference announcing the legislation, Governor Healey was joined virtually by Noah Kahan, who threw his support behind the measure: “I heard about what you’re announcing today and I just wanted to let you know how excited I am about it. The artist community and fans will greatly benefit from limiting ticket scalping and the sales of speculative tickets. I love my fans and want to protect them however I can. Artists alone could not tackle the market manipulation of secondary resellers. So, thank you so much for making this a priority in Massachusetts.”

Under the proposal, concert tickets cannot be resold for more than 110 percent of their original face value, unless an artist or venue explicitly authorizes a higher resale cap through a written agreement. For example, if a ticket originally cost $100, it could be resold for no more than $110.  

The bill limits the service fees charged by ticket resale marketplaces to no more than 10 percent of the listed resale price for sporting events and non-sporting events like concerts. For example, if a ticket is listed for resale on a resale platform for $300, the service fee charged by the resale platform cannot exceed $30. Today, many resale platforms charge service fees of roughly 20 percent or more, adding hundreds of dollars to the cost of tickets. This proposal is expected to cut resale service fees typically paid by consumers today in half.

The legislation also prohibits the sale of speculative tickets, meaning tickets that a seller does not actually have when they list them for sale. Too often, consumers pay for these tickets only to find out they are never delivered. During this summer’s World Cup matches at Gillette Stadium, some fans who purchased tickets through online resale platforms were turned away after discovering the tickets they bought never existed.

The bill includes additional consumer protections to prohibit deceptive resale websites that falsely suggest they are affiliated with artists or venues and to prevent resellers from misleading consumers about ticket availability or scarcity.

news_revere.title: TriF3cta Puts on a Great Show at Summer Concert Series
news_revere.author: Journal Staff
news_revere.summary:
Cary Shuman Photos

The musical group TriF3ecta delivered two entertaining hours of golden hits before a large audience at the Revere Summer Concert Series Sunday night on the American Legion Lawn.

The talented, high-energy trio of Joy Balzotti Granata, Ricki Erik, and John Kelly had the crowd dancing on its feet. The trio was in perfect unison vocal-wise and dance step-wise throughout its performance.

From the group’s stellar singing of ABBA’s “Dancing Queen” to Granata’s outstanding lead of the finale – appropriately enough Donna Summer’s classic “Last Dance” – the crowd showed its appreciation with hearty applause.

For the charismatic Granata, it was a happy homecoming as she grew up on Homer Street.

“I’m a proud graduate of Revere High School, Class of 1988,” said Granata,  “I love Revere. It will always be my home.”

Granata said the group has been busy all summer with several performances each week.

Asked to describe the group’s musical approach, she said, “We’re energetic, fun, loving, kind – we all have a different genre. We all work together and do a lot of rehearsing.”

Erik said the group loved the atmosphere for the show.

“We had a great time coming out and performing in Revere, which is a wonderful city,” said Erik, who in addition to his singing career plays the piano. “When I first came to Boston (from Florida) ten years ago, I lived on Mountain Avenue.”

Erik said he has a new original song debuting, “Miami Nights.” A previous song that he produced, “Como Te Llamas” merited consideration for a Grammy Award. 

Kelly was excited about the enthusiastic response to the group’s musical offerings. He made a trip into the audience to personally serenade fans with Kool and the Gang’s “Ladies Night.”

 “When I look at the schedule and I see Revere, I know it’s always a great place to perform,” said Kelly. “As a group, we work very well together. We’ve been performing a lot and we love it.”

news_revere.title: New ‘Green’ Distribution Center Proposed for McClellan Highway Targets LEED Platinum
news_revere.author: Journal Staff
news_revere.summary:
Staff Report

A 3.33-acre site along William F. McClellan Highway could soon be home to a state-of-the-art, 152,500-square-foot distribution center, according to new plans filed by Horizon/McClellan LLC. The proposed project will demolish an existing 21,144-square-foot, one-story warehouse and a surface parking lot to construct a modern, two-story Central Receiving and Distribution Center.

Located between Chelsea Creek and the CubeSmart Storage facility, the new 152,500-square-foot facility will be utilized primarily by Marketplace Development, which manages terminal concessions at Boston Logan International Airport. The building will be used to screen items before they are sent to the airport, replacing an older facility located less than a mile away at 290 McClellan Highway.

Key features of the proposed development include:

• A two-story building reaching approximately 55 feet in height.

• Anticipated uses including warehousing, receiving and distribution, and accessory offices.

• Off-street surface parking for approximately 10 vehicles.

• A total of 24 loading docks, eight of which will feature dedicated truck chargers to support fully electric transfers to the airport.

The project will also construct a limited-access extension of the Martin A. Coughlin Bypass Road to connect directly to the site. According to the development team, the facility is designed to be a leader in sustainability. It targets LEED Platinum certification, which would make it the first industrial building in New England to achieve this standard. By transitioning from diesel to an all-electric truck fleet for airport transfers, the project is estimated to reduce carbon dioxide emissions by approximately 68 tons per year.

Construction is projected to begin in the first quarter of 2027 and last approximately 18 months. Typical construction hours will be from 7:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m., Monday through Friday. No substantial sound-generating activity will occur before 7:00 a.m.

This filing is part of the Article 80B Large Project Review process. The public comment period for the 160 McClellan Highway project is open until Tuesday, August 18, 2026. Comments can be directed to Daniel Polanco at dan.polanco@boston.gov.

news_revere.title: Where is Teddy Roosevelt When We Need Him?
news_revere.author: Journal Staff
news_revere.summary:
The constant cacophony of bumbling babbling from our leaders in Washington these days with regard to the ongoing conflict with Iran brings to mind the wisdom of former President Theodore Roosevelt. On September 1, 1901 — just two weeks before he became President upon the assassination of President William McKinley — Roosevelt offered timeless foreign policy advice in a speech he delivered at the Minnesota State Fair:

“Speak softly and carry a big stick — you will go far. If a man continually blusters, if he lacks civility, a big stick will not save him from trouble; and neither will speaking softly avail, if back of the softness there does not lie strength, power. In private life there are few things more obnoxious than the man who is always loudly boasting; and if the boaster is not prepared to back up his words his position becomes absolutely contemptible. So it is with the nation. It is both foolish and undignified to indulge in undue self-glorification, and above all, in loose-tongued denunciation of other peoples.”

Today, the United States finds itself mired in a costly conflict with Iran. Even Israel, which has the most direct interest in subduing Iran, is sitting this one out, content to let the U.S. carry the ball.

Yet our leaders are pursuing a policy that is the antithesis of Roosevelt’s counsel. We boast loudly, but our diplomatic and military strategy lacks a true “stick” against an enemy comprised of zealots and fanatics who know they can outlast a traditional military campaign.

This approach fails to serve our national interests, threatens the stability of the global economy, and risks severe domestic financial fallout. Most importantly, the brave members of the military are putting their  lives on the line for a vague and ill-defined policy that has no clear military objective.

Now, as both Washington and Tehran dig in their heels following a collapsed truce, we must reject empty bluster. Our leaders must return to a strategy where measured diplomacy replaces pointless and endless bombing.

news_revere.title: The Miracle of a Bairn
news_revere.author: Journal Staff
news_revere.summary:
No, we are not Scottish. But we are big fans of the hit TV show Outlander, and “bairn,” the Scottish word for a newborn or a young child, has permanently entered our vocabulary.

Two weeks ago our family welcomed a bairn of our very own. Georgia, our first grandchild, is a beautiful baby girl named in honor of her maternal great-grandmother. Her arrival has cast our world in an entirely different light.

As adults, we take for granted the complex intricacies of our own bodies. By contrast, every feature of a newborn — from the tiny fingers and toes to the little nose — feels like a distinct, mesmerizing wonder.

Cradling Georgia in our arms brings an unparalleled sense of calm — a biological serenity that feels deeply imprinted into our ancient human DNA.

We are not particularly religious (despite 12 years of Catholic school). But if there is anything that might persuade us that a higher power exists in the universe, it is the miracle that is a new born baby.

news_revere.title: Guest Op-Ed: Massachusetts’ New Energy Rules will Recognize what Frontline Communities have Long Known: Across Massachusetts, Frontline Communities Fought for Rules that Recognize the Burdens Neighborhoods Already Carry
news_revere.author: Journal Staff
news_revere.summary:
By Roseann Bongiovanni

For over ten years, East Boston fought an Eversource substation proposed across from a children’s playground, beside Logan’s jet fuel tanks, on a flood-prone shoreline along Chelsea Creek. Despite overwhelming public opposition, the state approved the facility. But along the way, we exposed a permitting system stacked against the communities it most affected. In coalition with advocates and communities statewide, we organized to rewrite the rules – and this year, Massachusetts finalized them. 

Starting July 1, 2026, companies seeking to build many kinds of new energy infrastructure in Massachusetts – including fossil fuel power plants, gas pipelines, solar farms, battery storage sites, transmission lines, and substations – must complete what’s called a cumulative impact analysis before state approval. In plain terms: companies must look at what a community already lives with before the state lets them add anything new.  

Had this rule existed when Eversource proposed the substation, the question would have been different: not whether East Boston could prove harm, but whether the company could prove it would not add to the burdens we already carried. 

The assessment will cover 30 conditions, including air pollution, flood risk, heat exposure, and rates of asthma and heart disease. If a neighborhood ranks worse than the state median across the combined 30 conditions, the company can’t treat approval as routine. It must explain how it will avoid, reduce, or address the harm. And it must do so before key decisions are locked in, not after the bulldozers arrive. 

The old process assumed neighborhoods started from zero. East Boston didn’t. Lowell, Springfield, New Bedford – none of them did. Decades of unfair siting stacked power plants, fuel tanks, and waste facilities into the same ZIP codes, while the regulatory system treated each new project as if the last twenty hadn’t happened. The cumulative impact rule finally says: those projects are here, and they count. 

Alongside this requirement, the state created a grant program so communities can hire engineers, lawyers, and public health experts to scrutinize company claims. When Eversource came to East Boston, the multi-billion-dollar company arrived with attorneys, engineers, and consultants. Our neighborhood organized with what we had: volunteers working nights after their day jobs, neighbors donating money and meeting space, and pro bono legal representation from the Conservation Law Foundation. Together, we carried the fight to the Supreme Judicial Court.  

We were outspent and out-staffed at every turn. The new grants begin to correct a process that forced communities to scrape together resources while well-funded companies arrive ready to build. 

But the analysis isn’t limited to communities the state has already flagged: residents elsewhere can petition the state to require an analysis when local conditions aren’t fully captured by a mapping tool. And companies can no longer blur the line between actually reducing harm and offering a community benefit to offset it. A new park or playground cannot erase pollution, flood risk, or the safety concerns a project adds. 

Massachusetts has committed to building clean energy fast, and we should. But every project lands somewhere, and without rules like these, “somewhere” will be in places that follow the same unfair patterns that got us here. 

Not all energy projects carry the same risk. A new gas plant and a rooftop solar program warrant very different review, and the new rule is built to tell them apart. Every review should begin with the same question: what does this community already live with, and would this project make it worse? 

A rule on paper is only a beginning. The Energy Facilities Siting Board, which approves these projects, must prove this process is more than a checkbox for companies. That means taking these analyses seriously, weighing community petitions, and rejecting mitigation plans that dress up harm instead of preventing it. The agency’s record has not always inspired confidence – East Boston knows that firsthand. Residents, advocates, reporters, and legislators must keep watching as the first projects move through. 

East Boston did not stop the substation. But we helped change the rules that made that approval possible. That matters for East Boston and every community told to accept another project, burden, or sacrifice. The next neighborhood should not have to prove alone that its health, safety, and future count.

Roseann Bongiovanni writes on behalf of the Massachusetts Environmental Justice Table, a statewide coalition of community organizations and advocates working to advance environmental justice across the Commonwealth. She is Executive Director of GreenRoots.

news_revere.title: Metro Mayors Coalition’s 2026 Shannon Grant Summer Event at Rumney Marsh Academy
news_revere.author: Journal Staff
news_revere.summary:
By Jenifer Wallitsch

On July 10, more than 75 youth and over 30 adult volunteers, law enforcement officers, and community-based organization staff came together for the Metro Mayors Coalition’s 2026 Shannon Grant Summer Event at Rumney Marsh Academy in Revere. The event celebrated regional collaboration while strengthening positive relationships between youth, law enforcement, and community partners in support of reducing youth violence and gang involvement across Metro Mayors Coalition communities.

Youth from Braintree, Cambridge, Chelsea, Everett, Malden, Quincy, Revere, Somerville, and Winthrop participated in a full day of engaging activities designed to promote teamwork, wellness, and community connection. Throughout the day, participants enjoyed basketball, volleyball, flag football, indoor and outdoor arts and crafts, lawn games, fitness activities led by the Bruins Foundation, a youth-focused mental health presentation, music from the Mystic Valley YMCA Mobile Music Studio, and a community cookout led by Revere PAL. The event also welcomed Somerville Mayor Jake Wilson and Senator DiDomenico who stopped by to meet with participants and show their support for the program.

This year’s event marked several exciting milestones. For the first time, the Metro Mayors Coalition established a Youth Advisory Board (YAB) to help shape the vision and planning of the event. The YAB brought together youth representatives from across the region to provide ideas, offer feedback, and ensure the event reflected the interests and priorities of those it was designed to serve. During the opening ceremony, members of the Youth Advisory Board shared inspiring remarks about the importance of being included in the planning process and expressed their appreciation for having their voices heard.

The event also saw its strongest volunteer participation to date. Partners from both our Community Based Organizations and Police Departments provided enough volunteers to fully staff activity stations, creating more opportunities for meaningful interactions between youth, law enforcement officers, and community-based organization staff while ensuring activities were well supervised throughout the day. These informal conversations and shared experiences are a key component of the Shannon Grant’s mission to build trust, strengthen community relationships, and create positive connections with young people.

Since 2009, the Metro Mayors Coalition has hosted an annual summer event bringing together youth, law enforcement, and community-based organizations Image previewparticipating in the Metro Mayors Shannon Community Safety Initiative. This state-funded program, administered by the Executive Office of Public Safety and Security’s Office of Grants and Research (OGR), supports regional strategies to reduce gang involvement and youth violence through prevention, intervention, law enforcement collaboration, employment opportunities, and positive youth development. Each summer, the event rotates among coalition communities, providing youth with a fun, safe environment to build relationships and strengthen connections across the region.

For more information about the Metro Mayors Shannon Community Safety Initiative or the Metro Mayors Coalition, please contact Jenifer Wallitsch at jwallitsch@mapc.org.

news_communities.title: 67th Newport Folk Festival a hit
news_communities.author: Bill BrothertonBill BrothertonBill Brotherton
news_communities.summary:
NEWPORT, R.I. — Back in 1959, Lynn-born jazz impresario George Wein wanted to present Odetta and other folk singers in concert. But would the singers of spirituals, traditional, and political songs fit in at his renowned Newport Jazz Festival?

Probably.

But Wein noticed that folk music was gaining favor with America’s young adults and decided that Odetta and folkies like Pete Seeger and The Weavers deserved their own shindig. It was a hit.

Wein passed away in 2021, but the Newport Folk Festival is more popular than ever. Tickets sell out in minutes well before a single act has been announced.

The 67th annual NFF took place at Fort Adams State Park last Friday-Sunday. Performances take place on five stages daily — many overlap, meaning attendees are forever leaving in the middle of one performance and rushing to catch a bit of another. On Sunday, three of my must-see acts — Brandi Carlile, Tom Morello, and Kathleen Edwards — were on different stages at the same time.

Every year, rumors run wild that one superstar or another will perform unannounced. After all, who could have imagined that Dolly Parton, Paul Simon, and Joni Mitchell would magically appear on stage without warning.

This year, it was rumored that Taylor Swift would show up during Hayley Williams & Friends set on Friday. After all, they are BFFs and Williams attended the Taylor/Travis wedding.

Equally strong were speculations that Bruce Springsteen would sit in during Rage Against the Machine lead guitarist/political activist/rabble-rouser Morello’s Sunday set.

Neither happened, but there was no shortage of standout performances over the weekend. Yes, there was a special guest — Dave Matthews, who performed and danced with Joan Baez — during Sunday’s fest-closing set, hosted by Nathaniel Rateliff.

Every year I am most blown away by performers/bands that have escaped my radar. One — CMAT (the stage name of Ireland’s Ciara Mary-Alice Thompson) — on Sunday delivered the weekend’s best set, a high-energy, tightly choreographed hour that blended pop, indie, and alternative sounds and humor. “People tell me I remind them of an old Grecian god,” said the upfront frontwoman by way of introduction. One of her male guitarists wore women’s clothes: “This is Skirt Cobain,” she said. Delightful!

Evan Honer, backed by a rocking band, was a bundle of energy, racing around the stage and ending his set with a backflip. He is a great songwriter. “Enough happy songs,” he announced mid-set and delivered a solo-acoustic version of his “Mr. Meyers,” a heartbreaker about an older man grieving his late wife. Everyone around me was sobbing. I am tearing up just typing this. Check this guy out.

Women grabbed the spotlight on Friday, with many performers joining each other’s sets.

On the large Fort Stage, Lucy Dacus brought out some big names: Madi Diaz, Hayley Williams, Killers frontman Brandon Flowers, a duet of Jim Croce’s “Time in a Bottle.” Dacus was an amiable host and performer. Australian singer/songwriter/guitarist Courtney Barnett followed with a hard rock set that was hotter than the 90+ degree temperatures, and Courtney Marie Andrews won many new fans with her Americana/folk songs. LA-based folk/pop women-led trio Trousdale featured great harmonies, as did Boston trio Tiny Habits with its glorious cover of “Alone,” a hit for Heart.

Lily Fitts, a Topsfield native and Masconomet Regional High/UMass graduate now living in South Boston, wowed with well-written country-flavored tunes. “Lose You Now” and “I Don’t Owe You (Expletive)” have hit potential. Her parents Bill and Laurie were in the audience. They said her cover of Noah Kahan’s “Stick Season” on TikTok drew praise from Noah and impressed by her raw vocal style, Zach Bryan invited her to perform “Oklahoma City” in Los Angeles with him.

Other Newport highlights:

The Olllam (cq), a tight, expressive six-piece instrumental band whose members hail from Scotland, Ireland, and America wowed with jazzy grooves.

Amble, an Irish folk band, were also terrific, playing before a huge crowd. They played a great cover of John Prine’s “Angel From Montgomery” and their uptempo tunes would have had everyone dancing if there was room to move.

Cat Power (Chan Marshall) performed her groundbreaking 1996 album “The Greatest” from start to finish’ Fans were in heaven.

Gillian Welch and smiling hubby David Rawlings had a fine time performing Grateful Dead acoustic classics for an hour. Oh no… That earworm “Uncle John’s Band” is now stuck in my head. Darn!

Brittany Davis, who is blind, performed topical piano tunes that brought to mind Nina Simone.

The Grammy-winning Punch Brothers led by Chris Thile (mandolin), Noam Pikelny (banjo), and Chris Eldridge (guitar) amazed with their blend of bluegrass, classical, and folk. They were also hilarious. To wit: “We enjoy playing sea shanties,” said Thile. “We would now like to play a Sia Shanty” and he launched into the Australian singer-songwriter’s biggest hit: “I’m going to swing from the Chandelier.” They also performed the theme song from the movie “Jaws.”

The Lumineers gave a surprise show midday on Friday at the Bike Stage, where solar panels and festivalgoers riding bikes provide the electricity. It was a warmup for their headlining Saturday set and included a few hits and a superb cover of Bob Dylan’s “Subterranean Homesick Blues.” Newport Folk Executive Director Jay Sweet, an Essex resident, said he was impressed that attendees were so into the music that he saw only three people had their phones out to record a major band playing on such a tiny stage.

Canada’s Edwards, backed by a first-rate band, made her Newport debut 23 years after her debut album and was clearly having the time of her life, as was the large crowd that cheered her on with one ovation after another.

The overtly political Morello drew an enormous crowd that was more than ready to join in on his brutally powerful, hard-rocking Trump-bashing/pro-union/anti-fascist tunes. Woody Guthrie’s “This Land is Your Land” became a loud singalong. Even though Springsteen was a no-show, the former Rage Against the Machine lead guitarist’s cover of the boss’s “Ghost of Tom Joad” was a ferocious hard-rocking affair.

Ms. Lauryn Hill’s appearance was probably the most anticipated set of the entire festival, and it didn’t go smoothly. Her hour-long show was set to begin at 5:55 pm. The crowd clapped in anticipation and seats had been removed to give the large crowd room to dance. An emcee started playing Bob Marley’s “One Love” at about 6 p.m. Before long he was killing time, leading the audience in ridiculous time wasters/“Put your hands in the air” nonsense. It would be 31 minutes after her start time before Hill sang her first note. The crowd had started to thin out, heading to the main stage area to settle in for Hayley Williams & Friends. After three songs, none of which were the big hits, I left. I had another artist to write about, after all. Hill did sing a few of her Fugee and hit songs, I was told. When she was done she mingled with fans out near the merch stand, posing for selfies and signing autographs.

Williams’ friends included Jack Antonoff of Bleachers, Jenny Lewis of Rilo Kiley, Joy Oladokun, Remi Wolf, and many others. It was a blast.

news_communities.title: Peabody’s Family Fest returns to Emerson Park
news_communities.author: Anna BaughmanAnna BaughmanAnna Baughman
news_communities.summary:
PEABODY — Emerson Park will once again become a community gathering space for games, picnics, and family fun when the Peabody Education Foundation hosts its annual Family Fest on Saturday, Aug. 8 from 1-4 p.m. In the event of rain, Family Fest will be rescheduled to Sunday, Aug. 9 from 1-4 p.m.

For $10 per person and $20 maximum per family or group, attendees can enjoy afternoon activities including an inflatable obstacle course, face painting, music from a live DJ, and yard games out on the sprawling lawn. Food and drinks will be available for purchase, while adults can kick back and relax with wine and beer.

So far, the Peabody Education Foundation has received $7,800 in sponsorships from local businesses, families, and organizations. It is still seeking sponsors, and there are several opportunities to contribute: $1,000 supports one of Family Fest’s main attractions, $500 makes donors a community champion, $250 can support the snack stand or give a teacher a shout-out on social media, and $100 makes donors a family fun supporter. For more information, visit the PEF website, peabodyedfoundation.org.

Since 1985, the foundation has provided Peabody students with educational opportunities and resources that are beyond the budget of the school department.

PEF President and Chair Dave Gravel spearheaded Family Fest last year with the intent of raising funds for the organization’s grants program, which enhances student education through classroom projects, field trips, and much more. For example, Vice Chair Mary Bellavance said that PEF sponsors trips to museums and brings in guest speakers.

PEF has recently introduced a mental health program meant to address effects on children’s wellness after COVID. It also awards scholarships to high school seniors pursuing careers in education.

Last year, the foundation raised $130,000 just in grants for the Peabody education system. The board is hoping to invest $160,000 this year overall. The foundation’s team has no overhead, meaning that every penny raised goes into the many programs it offers.

When looking at the PEF’s impact over the years, it’s clear that the foundation has grown immeasurably.

“For a long time, people didn’t really know what PEF was, or understood the benefits of PEF,” Bellavance explained. “But over the last 10 years, we’ve been able to really get out and talk to the teachers more, talk to the schools.”

Community participation in events like Family Fest has been the backbone of the Peabody Education Foundation as they continue to grow and positively impact students’ lives.

news_communities.title: Peabody cadets win Ethics Bowl
news_communities.author: Amanda LureyAmanda LureyAmanda Lurey
news_communities.summary:
PEABODY — Two Peabody Veterans Memorial High School Air Force JROTC cadets returned home from a leadership program in Oklahoma with more than memories. Their team won first place in the Ethics Bowl competition, earning each member a $2,000 college scholarship.

Deputy Commander Meghan Burke and Operations Commander Elizabeth Hagerty, both incoming seniors, attended the Four Star Leadership program, hosted by Gen. Tommy Franks at the University of Central Oklahoma from July 18-23. The pair were among 75 students selected from more than 600 applicants worldwide to participate in the program.

Burke and Hagerty said the experience challenged them academically, strengthened their leadership abilities, and introduced them to lifelong friendships with students from across the country.

“I literally texted my mom the first night after the first speaker, and I was like, ‘My life is forever changed,’” Burke said. “It taught so much [about] how big problems aren’t that big, and they told us so many things about how you can be a leader.”

The program centers on what organizers call the “4 C’s” of leadership: character, common vision, communication, and caring. Hagerty said those principles were a major reason she decided to apply, after being encouraged by her AFJROTC instructors.

“After further research, I quickly realized that my personal values when it came to leadership aligned almost perfectly with the 4 C’s this program stands by,” Hagerty said.

Throughout the week, students attended presentations from military leaders, elected officials, and other accomplished speakers, while also participating in leadership exercises, writing persuasive speeches, and preparing for the Ethics Bowl.

Burke said one of the program’s biggest lessons was learning how to work through disagreements respectfully.

“You’re not supposed to make it into a debate at all,” Burke said of the Ethics Bowl. “You’re supposed to be finding a way for me to say my point, the other team to say their point, and then we agree on something.”

Weeks before arriving in Oklahoma, participants were assigned to six-person teams and given eight ethical scenarios to research. During the competition, teams analyzed two topics per match, attempting to reach common ground rather than defeat their opponents.

Burke and Hagerty’s team included three students from Oklahoma and one from Wyoming. After winning its preliminary matches, the team advanced to the finals and were ultimately crowned champions during the Annual Four Star Leadership Awards Banquet.

“We were shocked,” Hagerty said. “We knew we put in the work and had competitive arguments to make, but we didn’t know where other teams stood. … I’m more so happy that my team worked together, and it paid off.”

For Burke, the scholarship came as an unexpected bonus.

“I was just so proud of myself,” she said. “It really helped me realize that I am a leader, and I can do things in this world. It was just so amazing and so eye-opening. I looked right at my friend Elizabeth, and I was like, ‘We just did that.’”

Beyond the competition, both cadets said the program left a lasting impression through its demanding schedule, field trips to the Oklahoma National Memorial & Museum, the Oklahoma State Capitol, and the General Tommy Franks Leadership Institute and Museum, as well as the relationships they built with fellow participants and counselors.

“This program has changed who I was, developed who I am, and influenced who I am becoming,” Hagerty said. “I plan to apply to be a counselor next year to inspire upcoming leaders like I was.”

Both students also plan to continue pursuing military careers after graduating from PVMHS.

Burke has begun applying to the U.S. Air Force Academy, saying she hopes to continue developing as a leader through military service.

“I want to be able to lead people,” Burke said. “I want to be able to show that I had to earn my leadership, and I think the military really proves that… you wouldn’t have your position, you wouldn’t have your title, without the work.”

Hagerty plans to attend college, join Air Force ROTC, commission into the U.S. Air Force, and major in kinesiology or exercise science with the goal of becoming an Air Force physical therapist.

She also offered advice to younger students considering similar opportunities.

“Take that chance,” Hagerty said. “My favorite quote ever is: ‘If your dreams don’t scare you, they aren’t big enough.’ This quote couldn’t be any more true. Even when things scared me, I knew that I would regret it if I let my fears get the best of me.”

news_communities.title: Nahant plans for park improvements
news_communities.author: Erin HickeyErin HickeyErin Hickey
news_communities.summary:
NAHANT — Ecological restoration at Lodge Park is underway, accessibility improvements at Bailey’s Hill remain a priority, and Nahant is already beginning to look ahead to updating its Open Space and Recreation Plan years before the current one expires.

The Nahant Open Space and Recreation Plan Committee spent much of its Monday meeting reviewing progress on several ongoing conservation projects while beginning early discussions about updating the town’s Open Space and Recreation Plan, which expires in the spring of 2029.

One of the committee’s largest current initiatives is ecological restoration at Henry Cabot Lodge Park, where contractors recently began work funded through a Community Preservation Committee grant. Crews have started removing invasive woody vegetation, marking future pollinator gardens, and installing temporary signs to explain the work to visitors.

Committee Chair Trish Aldridge said five native pollinator gardens have already been staked out in locations where visitors will be able to easily see them once they’re planted.

“They also marked the five pollinator patches,” Aldridge said. “So we’re going to be planting plugs and seeds for the native pollinators. They picked visible locations so that when you were up in the meadow area walking around, you’d be able to see these patches.”

Planting is expected to take place later this year when cooler temperatures provide better growing conditions. Additional work targeting invasive Japanese knotweed is also planned.

The committee also discussed improvements planned for Bailey’s Hill, including a long-term goal of adding a wheelchair-accessible ramp to the gazebo. Although the current state-funded gazebo reconstruction project does not include funding for that ramp, members said they hope to pursue Community Preservation Committee funding during a future grant cycle.

Improving community access to Nahant’s open spaces, committee members said, remains an important goal.

“We’ve talked about wanting to do some more with accessibility and improving accessibility to open space in town,” Aldridge said. “Maybe this will be a small step in the right direction, something that’s doable.”

Committee members are also working with landscapers to incorporate native, rabbit-resistant pollinator plants around the rebuilt gazebo and are coordinating with local volunteers on future landscaping plans.

Another project moving forward is an interpretive panel highlighting Bailey’s Hill’s military history. Committee members are working with the Nahant Historical Society to obtain historic photographs and other materials for the display, which they hope will be installed near one of the former military bunkers overlooking the shoreline.

Committee member Paula Devereaux said the panel will help preserve a piece of Nahant’s history that could otherwise be forgotten.

“The military history… I think that as people get older and as the generations evolve, that there are going to be people who have no idea what that was for,” Devereaux said. 

Although Nahant’s current Open Space and Recreation Plan remains in effect until 2029, committee members said they want to begin planning early so the update process can move smoothly. The committee has contacted the Metropolitan Area Planning Council to better understand the timeline for updating the document and when the town should begin seeking technical assistance and funding.

“We’re not starting from scratch or anything,” Aldridge said. “We have a very good plan. It just will need to be updated as required.”

news_communities.title: Lynn roads will get a makeover
news_communities.author: Olivia HaydarOlivia HaydarOlivia Haydar
news_communities.summary:
LYNN — The condition of Lynn’s roads has been a frequent topic of discussion, and beginning July 29, five roads will undergo major improvements over the coming weeks. 

The Department of Public Works (DPW) plans to mill and repave the streets within two weeks. The work includes removing the existing asphalt and repaving the roads, eliminating potholes and cracks. 

The five roads scheduled for resurfacing are Tudor Street, from Nahant Street to the Lynnway; O’Callaghan Way, from Fecteau Way to Walnut Way; Holyoke Street, from Thorpe Road to Curwin Circle; Maple Street, from Western Avenue to Cross Street, including the intersection; and York Road, from Hilda Road to York Terrace. 

Parking access along the roads will be restricted, and detours and signage will be in place to redirect traffic during construction.

Every year, the DPW completes roadway resurfacing projects. The work is funded through Chapter 90, which is state funding allocated to cities and towns for their transportation infrastructure improvements, according to the Mass Gov website. 

For FY27, the Healey-Driscoll administration committed $300 million for the state of Massachusetts, which has been divided into two methods of distribution: $200 million for local road mileage, population, and employment, and $100 million solely distributed for local mileage roads. 

This means communities with more local road mileage receive a larger share of that funding. 

In Lynn, the local road mileage is more than 160 miles, the population is 101,253 people, and employment in the city includes 25,837 individuals. 

Out of the $200 million standard formula distribution, the city received $1,522,030.99, and out of the $100 million standard formula distribution, it received $529,830.18, which totals more than $2 million, according to the state’s apportionment spreadsheet. 

Lynn received more Chapter 90 funding than 335 of the state’s 352 cities and towns in Massachusetts. However, the top fund-receiving city is Boston with more than $17,000,000 allocated for FY27. 

Ward 1 City Councilor Dr. Pete D. Meaney shared how the projects within his ward will bring a better experience to all who commute on the roads every day. He shared that improving infrastructure has been a critical method that aids in the overall health and vitality of the city. 

“While we do not have the resources to repave every street that needs attention, the state funding we secured allows us to prioritize key thoroughfares with heavy traffic, including Maple Street and York Road,” Meaney said. “Completing this work will deliver smoother, safer roads that better serve residents and strengthen our city.” 

Ward 7 City Councilor Jordan T. Avery understands that road construction can be a temporary inconvenience to constituents along the roads in his ward, including O’Callaghan Way and Holyoke Street, but asks residents to maintain patience and cooperation for necessary work that will soon improve commuting. 

On O’Callaghan Way, Avery shared that there are three schools that see heavy traffic during school time: Lynn Classical High School, Breed Middle School, and Julia F. Callahan School. This roadwork will improve safety and remove potential hazards before students return to school this fall. 

“This is important work that needs to move forward, and these will provide smoother roadways for motorists, vehicles, pedestrians, school buses, and even our emergency vehicles… It’s been kind of neglected, you know, for a little bit and definitely needs those repairs,” Avery said. 

Avery backed Meaney’s statement on the fact that many roads in Lynn need revamping, but that these five roads are the right step in the right direction to fix travel on some of the busiest roads in the city. 

The list of roads was finalized several months ago, Avery said, and the choice was a group effort between the Mayor’s office, DPW, and City Councilors who hear the concerns regularly from their constituents. 

The DPW Commissioner had not responded to requests for comment by print deadline. 

Avery said that when issues arise from residents, they go directly to those who can make the improvements, like DPW in this situation of road infrastructure. 

“We hear firsthand from our residents, and we take those concerns each and every time I meet with the commissioner,” Avery added. “If it’s with the mayor’s office, if it’s with his chief of staff, if it’s with the city planner, I continue to advocate and fight for our residents and our wards, making sure that we’re investing in our roadways and making sure that it’s being appropriated correctly into areas that need it most.”

news_communities.title: Saugus’ Tribu liquor license in limbo
news_communities.author: Elizabeth Della PianaElizabeth Della PianaElizabeth Della Piana
news_communities.summary:
SAUGUS — The Alcoholic Beverages Control Commission held a hearing for Tribu Mexican Bar and Grill, the restaurant that served Hernan Ramon Marrero alcoholic drinks after hours between May 5 and 6 before he got into his car, drove southbound in the northbound lanes, and crashed into Massachusetts State Trooper Kevin Trainor. Both men died in the accident.

During the hearing, it was revealed that Marrero was a “father figure” to Tribu’s manager, Herman Zambrano, who broke his two-year sobriety during the period covered by the investigation.

Attorney Henry DiGiacomo noted the violations that the ABCC would be reviewing: Permitting an illegality on the licensed premises, which violated Mass General Laws Chapter 138 Section 12 Sale of an alcoholic beverage after the hour fixed by the local licensing authorities (26 counts); No licensee or employee or agent of a license shall offer or deliver any free drinks to any person or group of persons (31 counts); and permitting a disorder in or on the licensed premises.

Tribu’s attorney, Tracy Firicano, noted in her opening statement that all of the violations stem from one night, and that no other violations have occurred against the restaurant.

“The collective violations initially before the board here today occurred within a concentrated period of time, more or less about two hours. And they did involve staff members who were in receipt of some of the beverages, and only one customer, Mr. Marrero,” Firicano said.

DiGiacamo called ABCC Supervising Investigator Caroline Guarino to the stand to go over the events of Tuesday, May 5 leading into early Wednesday morning.

Guarino said that on May 8, investigators arrived at Tribu, where they noted the posted hours of operation for Monday through Wednesday, which were 11 a.m. to midnight.

Zambrano was there to speak to investigators, and later contacted owners Paul Mongui and Abner Gonzalez for Guarino, who later arrived.

On May 15, with the help of the restaurant’s video surveillance technician, Mongui and Gonzalez provided footage to investigators.

Guarino then provided the ABCC with a timeline of events that unfolded using surveillance footage and a guest check.

Marrero arrived at Tribu at 9:15 p.m. on Tuesday, receiving his alcoholic beverage at 9:20 p.m. from bartender Charity Jimenez. He would then order food at 9:37 p.m. from bartender Héctor Ospina Valencia. This beverage and food would be added to the guest check.

At 9:53 p.m., Marrero received his food, and at 10 p.m., he finished his first beverage. Marrero received his second alcoholic beverage at 10:01 p.m., which was also on the guest check.

At 10:50 p.m., Zambrano is seen speaking with Marrero, and the manager ordered two old fashioned beverages. This drink was Marrero’s third and his first free one. Between 11:36 p.m. and 12:53 a.m. Marrero would receive six more drinks, all free.

Through 1:34 a.m., staff members were observed being served multiple alcoholic beverages by Valencia, leading to 31 free drinks and 26 drinks after hours.

During an interview with Valencia on May 15, Guarino asked Valencia how Marrero paid for his drinks, and Valencia said that Zambrano told him the drinks were on the house.

Firicano pointed out that Marrero was not a typical customer during her cross-examination of Guarino.

“They (Marrero and Zambrano) had been friends for 20 years, and Mr. Marrero was something of a mentor to Mr. Zambrano,” Firicano said.

In her closing statement, Firicano also said that, based on interviews with staff, there was no proof that after-hours drinking and free drinks were a normal occurrence at the restaurant. Guarino confirmed that staff she interviewed said they had never seen this happen.

She continued that Mongui, Gonzalez, and Zambrano were three hardworking men who knew each other for many years and provided investigators with everything they needed. She also said that the restaurant had already implemented additional measures to ensure nothing like this happened again.

“Two people lost their lives here. … Now that’s a tragedy. There’s no question that that’s a tragedy for all involved. And as human beings, it’s difficult not to let emotion permeate what is being assessed. However, the issues before you, honorable commission members, are very narrow ones,” Firicano said. “And that doesn’t minimize the tragedy. … I would ask that the commission also orient this incident within the context of both the restaurant’s history and the background of the owners.”

In his closing statement, DiGiacomo listed four other cases in which the ABCC had found other defendants in violation.

The first case was Rum Runners Inc. v. the ABCC, where the appeals court found the licensee responsible if the illegal act was visible to staff or if staff knew or should have known about it.

The second case was Rico’s of the Berkshires Inc. v. ABCC, where the appeals court found that the responsibility of the licensee is to exercise sufficient close supervision so that there is compliance with the law on the premises.

The third case was Burlington Package Liquors Inc. v. ABCC, where the appeals court found that a licensee who sells alcohol is “found at his own peril to keep within the condition of the license.”

The fourth case was Profile Lounges Inc. v. ABCC, where the appeals court confirmed that hours of sale are a condition imposed by the local licensing authority; therefore, delivery after hours would be a violation of license conditions.

The ABCC is set to issue a ruling at a later date.

news_communities.title: Holly Sklar: America needs a raise
news_communities.author: Guest CommentaryGuest CommentaryGuest Commentary
news_communities.summary:
Holly Sklar

People who work for a living need to be able to make a living. Raising the minimum wage is a vital part of the solution to the affordability crisis.

The cost of food, housing, and other necessities has risen sharply. But the federal minimum wage has been stuck at $7.25 since July 24, 2009. That’s 17 years with the same minimum wage, but a much higher cost of living.

Full-time work at $7.25 an hour amounts to just $15,080 if you are paid for 40 hours a week, 52 weeks a year.

The economy has grown since 2009, but the federal minimum wage has not. A red light for minimum wage is a green light for increasing inequality.

Workers’ share of national income is at record lows while corporate profits are at record highs.

The minimum wage keeps falling further behind the rising cost of living. The federal minimum wage peaked in buying power way back in 1968, when it was worth $15.62 in 2026 dollars, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics Inflation Calculator. Millions of workers make less than that today.

Nationally, 14 million workers make less than $15 per hour and 20 million workers make less than $16, including overtime, tips, and commissions, according to the Economic Policy Institute’s Low Wage Workforce Tracker.

Twenty states have minimum wages no higher than the $7.25 federal level: Alabama, Georgia, Idaho, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, New Hampshire, North Carolina, North Dakota, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, Wisconsin, and Wyoming.

Five of those states — Alabama, Louisiana, Mississippi, South Carolina, and Tennessee — don’t have a state minimum wage, and in Georgia and Wyoming, the state minimum is $5.15, so the federal $7.25 minimum wage applies.

The minimum wage matters for workers making the minimum, and it matters for workers making more than the minimum, but still not earning enough to make ends meet.

For example, the median hourly wage for home health and personal care aides in 2025 was just $10.83 in Louisiana and $11.65 in Texas, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The median wage is the midpoint in wages, not the bottom. The median wage for childcare workers was $10.60 in Mississippi and $10.92 in Alabama. Half of those workers earn less than those amounts.

In Pennsylvania, the $13.85 median hourly wage for fast food cooks was much lower than the $17.20 median wage for fast food cooks in neighboring New York. New York has increased minimum wages multiple times since 2013 while Pennsylvania has stayed stuck at $7.25. Comparing counties on both sides of the state border, the Keystone Research Center reported that “leisure and hospitality employment growth in New York far outpaced Pennsylvania’s.”

Raising the minimum wage will help workers keep up with the cost of living and bolster the consumer spending that businesses and the economy depend on.

It’s important to remember that workers are also customers.

Raising the minimum wage is a very efficient way to boost businesses and the economy because it puts more money in the pockets of people who most need to spend it.

Fairer pay also helps business by reducing costly employee turnover and improving productivity and customer service.

Employees often make the difference between repeat customers and lost customers.

Decades of rigorous research of actual minimum wage increases show that raising the minimum wage is beneficial and does not cause job loss.

There’s nothing radical about a decent minimum wage. As Adam Smith, the “father of modern capitalism,” put it in 1776, “It is but equity, besides, that they who feed, clothe, and lodge the whole body of the people, should have such a share of the produce of their own labor as to be themselves tolerably well fed, clothed, and lodged.”

Holly Sklar is the CEO of Business for a Fair Minimum Wage, a national network of business owners and executives who believe fair pay makes good business sense. www.businessforafairminimumwage.org.

news_communities.title: Letter: Beccia’s record deserves a fair reading
news_communities.author: To the editorTo the editorTo the editor
news_communities.summary:
To the editor: 

I am responding to the July 13 letter in the Daily Item by. Jim Walsh. He endorsed an opponent of my candidate, John Beccia. As a longtime political advisor and manager, I have a couple of objections to his description of John. 

First, without attribution or any proof offered, he asserts that John is some sort of mysterious crypto operator. He then pivots to Donald Trump’s personal fortune and never comes back. By the time he is finished, he has told us nothing about John Beccia. Not a statement was offered, not a position, not a single fact. That is playing fast and loose with a serious accusation. 

Second, there is nothing mysterious here because John has never hidden any of it. He is a lawyer who spent his career on the regulation and compliance side of finance. He was tapped by the U.S. Treasury to serve on committees that examine rules to protect against money laundering and illicit activity for digital assets which were issues he worked on with traditional financial services companies for many years. He worked with state regulators on the first state licensing rules for that industry in the country because someone had to protect consumers before people got hurt. He has advised several companies on how to acquire proper licensing and develop compliance programs to protect against bad actors. Finally, he has taught cryptocurrency regulation at Boston University School of Law.  

He has disclosed every asset he owns in a public filing down to the last municipal bond for any voter in this district to read. When John talks about that industry, he talks about rules, transparency, and accountability because building those was his job. 

There is a difference between spending a career putting guardrails on a new industry and being owned by one. John’s case rests on a public record and a public disclosure. Mr. Walsh’s rests on neither. 

My expectation is that Mr. Walsh will reconsider the error of his ways. Do I think John will bring much needed and hard-earned wisdom to the job of Representative of the Sixth District? 

You betcha/Beccia! 

Victor L’Esperance

Lynn
